eyebrow: Eat Like a Local in Ranong · Updated 2026
intro: Ranong is a small town where great food hides around every corner — from bold Southern Thai curries and fresh Andaman seafood to morning dim sum and roti with curry. We've rounded up 10 restaurants that locals and travellers talk about most, with signature dishes, prices, and neighbourhood guides so your next meal in Ranong is a hit from the very first bite.

blocks.html:
Ranong sits on the border between the Andaman Sea and Myanmar, so the food here is a beautiful mash-up of influences. Bold Southern Thai cooking meets super-fresh seafood hauled up from the estuary, with morning dim sum and roti-with-curry that have been woven into the town's eating culture for generations. Stroll through the old quarter around Khao Niwet and you'll catch the heady scent of shrimp paste drifting out of Southern kitchens; drive out to Pak Nam and you can sit over a plate of grilled shellfish with a cool sea breeze coming off the water; if you want atmosphere, there's even a creek-side café tucked into the forest. All of it is within a few minutes' drive of each other in this compact little province.

Many restaurants on this list are names locals have been loyal to for decades — Khun Lin, which has stood beside the town for over twenty years, with its talum phuk fish and stir-fried bai liang with egg; Thod Rong Thao, which has swept up multiple Wongnai Users' Choice awards for honest Southern cooking with quality ingredients; Keinglay, the seaside seafood landmark at Pak Nam for watching the sunset; Roti Nissara in Ban Ngao, where queues start early because the roti sells out fast; and Baan Rai Ia Arun in Kapoe, where khao nom jin with three curry dips sits beside a stream running through the jungle. Each place earns its reputation plate by plate. Read on to find out which restaurant is right for which meal.

blocks.name: Khun Lin Restaurant
blocks.signature: Talum Phuk Fish (Pla Talumphuk), stir-fried bai liang with egg, tom yum seafood, prawns in tamarind sauce
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Ranong to soak at Raksawarin Hot Spring, the restaurant right across the road is Khun Lin — a Southern Thai seafood place that has been part of the town's fabric for over twenty years. It started as a tiny coffee shop and grew into somewhere both locals and visitors fill almost every day. The setting is lush with trees and mountain views, with a mix of wooden and marble tables, making it a solid choice for a family's first dinner or a relaxed evening after exploring Ranong's old quarter.

The dish that comes up again and again in reviews is the pla talumphuk (the restaurant lists it as Pla Hlumphuk Lui Suan): the flesh is silky soft, the bones are fried so crisp you can eat the whole fish, and it's dressed with a fresh herb salad. The stir-fried bai liang with egg is a local staple done just right — not too dry, not too wet. Anyone who wants heat should try the tom yum seafood, fiery and punchy, with bouncy fresh prawns; and the tamarind-glazed prawns, the priciest item on the menu, balance sweet, sour, and savoury beautifully. Other favourites include deep-fried mackerel with shrimp paste and egg-and-crab-roe nam phrik, both outstanding with steamed rice.

Prices start around 60 THB a dish, with most dishes in the low hundreds. Larger seafood items like the tamarind prawns climb to several hundred THB, and the average spend is around 150–250 THB per person — very reasonable for fresh Andaman seafood. The restaurant is open every day from morning through evening. One extra draw: there are plenty of photogenic spots in the garden, plus quirky little interactive touches like fortune-stick oracle menus and wishing-doll figurines, which make it as much a check-in stop as a meal.

Worth noting: some reviews say the flavour skews a touch tourist-friendly. If you prefer the full-on Southern Thai heat of the original style, ask for extra phrik nam pla on the side. Crowds can slow the kitchen on public holidays. Pla talumphuk is available only when the kitchen can source it — ask the staff when you arrive. Overall this is a restaurant Ranong locals keep recommending to newcomers, and the location right next to the hot spring makes it the easiest first stop in town.
mustOrder: Talum Phuk Fish (Pla Hlumphuk Lui Suan)
blocks.bestFor: Your first meal in Ranong after soaking at the hot spring; great for families

blocks.name: Thod Rong Thao
blocks.signature: Prawns stir-fried with shrimp paste and stink beans, prawns in tamarind sauce, soft-shell crab fried with garlic, turmeric-fried sand whiting, stir-fried bai liang
blocks.descHtml:
If you want Southern Thai food exactly as it's cooked in Ranong homes, Thod Rong Thao — known locally as the Rong Kluang shop — is the first name you'll hear from anyone who lives here. The restaurant occupies an old wooden shophouse in the old quarter on Kitphadueng Road, near the Governor's Mansion. You pass through the kitchen to reach the tables at the back. The name comes from the days when the floor was made from areca-palm sheathing and guests had to remove their shoes before stepping up; the floor is concrete now and you can keep your shoes on. This is the ideal spot for a first meal in town if you want honest, unfussy local food at its best.

Nearly every table orders the prawns stir-fried with shrimp paste and stink beans — fragrant shrimp paste, crisp stink beans, fresh prawns, the sweet-salty-savoury balance of the South all in one wok. Follow that with the tamarind prawns, pleasantly sour-sweet; the soft-shell crab fried with garlic, praised across reviews as the star of the show — crispy outside, tender inside; and the turmeric-fried sand whiting, so crisp you can eat it whole straight from the fryer. Vegetable lovers get stir-fried bai liang with egg and spicy sour fish curry alongside rice.

The overall flavour profile is genuinely Southern Thai: punchy, sour, salty, the works. Most reviews praise consistent seasoning and fresh ingredients, especially the prawns and fish from nearby waters. Dishes start in the low dozens of baht, with meals averaging 100–250 THB per person — excellent value for the quality of seafood. Multiple consecutive Wongnai Users' Choice awards speak for themselves.

The restaurant is small — fewer than ten tables — and it gets hot inside the wooden house at lunch and on weekends. If you're coming as a group or for a special meal, it's worth calling ahead. Street parking is available in front and along the wall. Open every day 11:00–20:00; the mid-afternoon lull tends to be the most relaxed time to visit.
mustOrder: Prawns stir-fried with shrimp paste and stink beans
blocks.bestFor: First meal in Ranong; the real deal for bold Southern Thai food
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: seafood · Andy Li / Wikimedia (CC0)

blocks.name: Ranong O Cha Dim Sum
blocks.signature: Steamer baskets of dim sum, pork congee, bak kut teh, pan-fried egg, sticky rice dumplings (ba chang), steamed rice with preserved vegetables
blocks.descHtml:
Ask a Ranong local where to eat this morning and Ranong O Cha is almost guaranteed to be the first answer. This long-standing dim sum shop on Chaloem Phra Kiat Road, on the way to the fish market, has been part of Ranong life for generations — people here grew up eating dim sum here from childhood all the way to grandparent age. It's the ideal place to begin your first day in the province with a proper Chinese-style breakfast. The building is a vintage shophouse with both air-conditioned indoor seating and tables outside.

The ordering system is fun: you walk up to the chiller cabinet, pick your own steamer baskets, note your table number, and the staff steam everything fresh for you; other dishes you order at the table. Must-orders include the dim sum basket selection (har gow, siu mai, and more from the cabinet), pork congee and salted-egg congee (silky and aromatic, by all accounts), bak kut teh served piping hot, the pan-fried egg, sticky rice dumplings (ba chang), and steamed rice with preserved vegetables. The house dipping sauce — a sweet-sour blend — gets a special mention in multiple reviews.

Most reviewers agree: the dim sum here has more punch than many competitors — thin skins, dense fillings, fresh ingredients. One reviewer simply wrote 'almost everything is delicious.' And the prices are extremely kind: baskets are around 25 THB each, and congee or rice dishes run 60–75 THB. Two people can eat a full meal for a few hundred baht. The Google rating sits around 4.1 stars from thousands of reviews — a consistent crowd-pleaser.

The restaurant opens early, around 06:30, and closes early afternoon. Bestsellers sell out fast; arriving after 10:00 a.m. risks missing the top baskets. Come early, load up your tray in one trip to avoid multiple steaming waits, and settle in for the most Ranong morning possible.
mustOrder: Dim sum baskets (har gow / siu mai)

blocks.name: Roti Nissara
blocks.signature: Crispy-outside soft-inside roti with chicken massaman curry, Southern-style khao yam, fried chicken, salad with peanut dressing, iced tea
blocks.descHtml:
If roti is your thing and you're making the trip to Ranong, every local voice will point you to Roti Nissara — a small halal breakfast spot near the Ban Ngao fresh market, close to Phu Khao Ya hill. It's been open long enough to become one of those places people say you haven't really been to Ranong if you missed it. The star is the roti dough, kneaded in-house with a milky-buttery fragrance, fried over a medium flame to just the right crunch on the outside and softness inside. It's the perfect way to fuel up before heading out to explore.

The most popular order is roti dipped into chicken massaman curry — the chicken falls-off-the-bone tender and the spiced coconut gravy soaks into the warm roti perfectly. Wongnai reviews consistently back this up: 'genuinely crispy-outside-soft-inside roti with massaman, really delicious.' Southern-Thai khao yam is next — tossed with budu fish sauce, it delivers all four notes: sour, salty, sweet, spicy at once. There's also crispy fried chicken with sticky rice, salad with aromatic peanut dressing, and iced tea to finish. Pre-packaged roti is even available as a take-home gift.

Prices are very friendly — a plain roti is a matter of a few dozen baht, and a full person can walk away well-fed for under 100 THB. The place is a small, homey shopfront with parking. Key thing to know: this spot is popular and busy, and on weekend mornings you may wait a bit — roti is fried fresh, one sheet at a time. Come early for the best selection.

Located on Prachaphithak Road, Tambon Ngao, on the route up to Phu Khao Ya hill. Open every day 08:00–13:00 only — morning to early afternoon. Plan to stop here for breakfast before climbing Phu Khao Ya or visiting the waterfalls nearby. Consistent flavour, low prices, and a genuinely Southern-style roti you won't find many other places — that's the combination that keeps this spot full.
blocks.bestFor: Breakfast before heading up Phu Khao Ya
blocks.spice: Khao yam / curry is bold Southern-style; adjustable

blocks.name: Keinglay Ranong
blocks.area: Pak Nam, Mueang Ranong District, Ranong
blocks.signature: Yellow curry with sea bass, steamed sea bass with lime, yam kung khaei, soft-shell crab stir-fried with kachek noodles, Burmese bean salad
blocks.descHtml:
Keinglay Ranong is the seafood restaurant by the sea that Ranong locals book as the dinner destination almost every time they have guests in town. The restaurant sits at the end of Pak Nam Road — drive along the coast out of town for a few minutes and you'll find a tall, airy open-air pavilion facing the water, with a clear view across to Ko Song (Myanmar's Kawthaung) island on the other side. Fishing boats and cargo ships glide in and out to watch. For a relaxed seafood dinner with a cool breeze and a stunning outlook, this is hard to beat for families or groups of friends.

Almost every table orders the yellow curry with sea bass — Southern-style, punchy sour and spicy — alongside the steamed sea bass with lime, the fish firm and the zesty sauce hitting every note. Other dishes that stand out: yam kung khaei, a vibrant salad with Ranong shrimp paste adding a particular local depth; soft-shell crab stir-fried with kachek noodles — crispy outside, tender inside; and the Burmese bean salad (yam tua phama), a flavour specific to this border region you won't find easily elsewhere. Most reviews praise the freshness of the ingredients, the careful preparation, and the beautiful plating.

Prices are fair for the view and quality — around 250–500 THB per person, with individual dishes starting from the low hundreds. The Google rating sits around 4.4 stars from more than 1,800 reviewers, showing this is a restaurant both locals and visitors come back to. Staff are fast and friendly, which also gets regular mentions.

Open every day around 11:00–21:00. The best time to come is the evening before sunset — you get the golden light over both the Thai and Myanmar shorelines. Midday can be harsh in the sun. If you're coming in a large group or during a festival weekend, call ahead to book a table by the water. Plenty of parking. You can also walk down to the beach in front of the restaurant.
mustOrder: Soft-shell crab stir-fried with kachek noodles
blocks.bestFor: Sunset dinner by the sea; families and groups of friends

blocks.name: Baan Rai Ia Arun
blocks.signature: Khao nom jin with 3 curry dips, Southern Thai home dishes, refreshing drinks by the creek
blocks.descHtml:
Baan Rai Ia Arun is a farmstay, café, and Southern Thai home-cooking restaurant hidden in a valley in Kapoe District, about 25 km from the town centre and Ranong Airport. The owner is an architect who returned to transform the family orchard into a nature retreat. The setting is the main draw: a clear stream runs through the grounds, the buildings are made from natural materials, seating is scattered through the garden with plenty of photogenic spots, and there's a quiet that's hard to find elsewhere. It's perfect for a peaceful lunch stop along the way, a couple wanting to sit and unwind, or a family with children who want to wander in the garden.

The dish most often mentioned in reviews is the khao nom jin set with three curry dips — about 60 THB per set — which comes with coconut milk, fish offal (tai pla), and nam phrik dips in one serve, alongside fresh garden vegetables and edible flowers. Multiple real reviews agree: 'delicious in every dip.' The home-cooking menu also includes yam pak kud (fern-shoot salad), pandan-flower omelette, bai liang stir-fried with egg, bai liang in coconut milk soup, salt-fried pork belly, and fresh nam phrik with farm vegetables. Finish with a refreshing drink by the stream.

Prices sit around 101–250 THB per person. A few reviewers note it's slightly more than a typical local home-cooking spot, but most feel that fresh farm ingredients and the surroundings justify it. The restaurant and café open around 08:00–17:00 every day. It gets busy on weekends, and sometimes seating is tight and queues form. For a calm experience, go on a weekday or early in the morning.

This place has become a Ranong landmark that travellers specifically stop for, combining a stay, a meal, and a garden café under one roof — Southern Thai food served sharp and bold with a full view of nature all around. Note: the access road goes into a valley, so driving yourself is easiest. The accommodation wing is private — please keep to the garden and restaurant areas unless you're staying.
mustOrder: Khao nom jin with 3 dips (coconut milk / tai pla / nam phrik)
Fresh nam phrik with farm vegetables
blocks.bestFor: Lunch by the creek; café lovers; couples and families

blocks.name: Somboon Pochana
blocks.signature: Stir-fried bai liang with egg, yellow-curry crab, fish-sauce-fried sea bass, stir-fried stink beans with shrimp paste and prawns, sour curry with sea bass
blocks.descHtml:
Somboon Pochana is one of Ranong's long-standing seafood restaurants, on Phetkasem Road in the town centre. It's been open long enough to become the name locals think of when they want proper sit-down seafood in air-conditioning. If you're staying near Raksawarin Hot Spring, it's a short drive. Good for families and groups of friends alike.

The dish the restaurant is best known for is yellow-curry crab — a long-standing house speciality with fragrant curry powder, firm crab meat, and a pot of steamed rice to go with it. Follow that with stir-fried bai liang with egg (the indispensable local vegetable of the South), a large fish-sauce-fried sea bass with crispy skin, stir-fried stink beans with shrimp paste and prawns (with a distinct shrimp-paste aroma), and sour curry with sea bass that multiple reviewers describe as 'fragrant spicy, well-rounded spicy' with generous fish and a full-tasting broth. The shrimp-paste-based nam phrik with fresh crudités is another crowd favourite with rice.

According to real Wongnai reviews, the restaurant scores around 3.8 stars — a sign of mixed but positive feedback. The sour curry, stink-bean stir-fry, and nam phrik are consistently praised; a few reviews note that some stir-fried greens can skew bland. The straightforward advice: lead with the curry dishes and shrimp-paste dishes for the best value. Most dishes are 101–250 THB per person; larger or premium fish dishes climb above that according to size.

The setting is a shophouse dining room along the road — air-conditioned inside, with plenty of tables — old-school and unpretentious but comfortable and mosquito-free. Open every day around 11:00–21:30. Located beside Thai Samut Insurance on Phetkasem Road and easy to find. Evenings can get busy; ordering a spread to share across the table is the best way to go.
mustOrder: Stir-fried stink beans with shrimp paste and prawns
blocks.bestFor: Groups and families; order seafood to share
blocks.spice: Medium (sour curry / shrimp-paste dishes are spicy; adjustable on request)
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: seafood · Andy Li / Wikimedia (CC0)

blocks.name: Pa Ratree Som Tam (Som Tam Dan)
blocks.signature: Blue crab som tam 3-flavour, horseshoe-crab egg salad, salted-egg corn som tam, blue crab clear noodle soup, grilled chicken
blocks.descHtml:
If you want som tam as spicy and direct as the people of the South and Northeast eat it, locals in Ranong point to Pa Ratree Som Tam — nicknamed Som Tam Dan because it's near the Dan health clinic on Tha Mueang Road in the Khao Niwet neighbourhood. It's a simple, no-frills Isan-style shop; the décor doesn't aim for anything, but Pa Ratree's hands are what keep people coming back. Perfect for a sharp, sour, energising lunch.

The most talked-about dish is the blue crab som tam — review after review agrees: 'blue crab is generous, the crabs are fresh and sweet,' pounded to a three-flavour balance of sour, salty, and sweet. The other regional speciality is horseshoe-crab egg salad alongside salted-egg corn som tam, the salty richness of the egg playing against the sweetness of the corn. For a hot bowl, the blue crab clear noodle soup is the natural partner. The grilled chicken is freshly grilled, the smoke drifting out early in the day. Multiple reviewers praise that the kitchen uses fresh lime on every dish and goes light on MSG.

Prices are very approachable — most dishes start from 40 THB, and two or three people can eat well under a hundred baht each. That's why students, office workers, and families in town eat here regularly. The restaurant is in central Ranong, easy to find, with roadside parking. Opens around 10:00 to early evening (approximately 17:00).

Worth noting: lunch rush means popular items move fast — blue crab in particular is best ordered by around midday, or you may miss it. If you can't sit in, the restaurant also delivers and takes phone orders at 077-880-570. Spice level is adjustable. A genuine local favourite.

blocks.name: Baan Nai Mong Treehouse (Cafe Naimong)
blocks.signature: Drinks and cakes in a creek-side forest café, snacks, forest photo spots
blocks.descHtml:
Baan Nai Mong Treehouse (Cafe Naimong) is a forest creek-side café tucked just ten minutes by car from central Ranong. Nai mong means 'forest' in Southern Thai dialect — this is quite literally a little house in a big forest. There's both a treehouse stay and a café section open to drop-in visitors. It's ideal for anyone wanting to escape for a few hours, breathe clean air, sit by running water, and watch ducks and fish go about their business while friendly dogs and cats wander over. Photography lovers and anyone after a quiet mental reset will feel completely at home here.

The coffee crowd's favourite is the coconut-blossom-syrup Americano — gently sweet and floral, balancing nicely against the bitterness. The dessert side offers honey toast that reviewers say is drizzled with genuinely fresh honey, and cakes including red velvet and white-chocolate fudge praised for their softness. For savoury snacking there's som tam, fish-sauce-fried chicken wings, and fresh-fruit smoothies — watermelon, pineapple, passion fruit with mint — in multiple combinations. More than one reviewer has said that everything tastes better when you're eating while watching the stream.

The atmosphere is the real selling point: a rope bridge swings across the creek for photos, glass walls frame the surrounding greenery, there's a bamboo grove, clear water, and multiple seating zones both by the water and inside the building. Groups have board games to pass the time. Prices are mid-range at about 101–250 THB per person, accessible without overthinking it.

Open every day 09:30–20:30. The entrance road is a little narrow but parking is available. Reviews note that the stream is at its most beautiful during the rainy season and monsoon; in the dry season water levels drop. For the best creek shots, avoid dry season; mornings and late afternoons when the light softens are the most comfortable times to sit outside.
blocks.bestFor: Café lovers wanting to sit by a creek in the forest and take photos

blocks.name: Krua Mango & Milkgo Café
blocks.signature: Prawns in tamarind sauce with sweet-sour balance, stir-fried bai liang with egg, Southern Thai seafood
blocks.descHtml:
Krua Mango & Milkgo Café is a Southern Thai-seafood restaurant in Ranong's Khao Niwet neighbourhood that locals and travellers alike pin as one of their first meals when arriving in the province. The building is a glass-and-open-air structure — there's both an air-conditioned indoor zone and outdoor seating with a cooling breeze — set in a wide lot with a football pitch and plenty of easy parking. Good for families and large groups. If you want honest Ranong Southern Thai cooking in a comfortable, spacious environment, this delivers.

The must-order is the tamarind prawns — large prawns fried with shells on, glazed in a well-balanced sweet-sour tamarind sauce. Real reviews agree: 'fresh prawns and the sauce hits just right.' The bai liang stir-fried with egg is indispensable — this local leafy vegetable is done soft and sweet, perfectly matched with the egg. Southern Thai curry fans should try the mango curry and the sour curry with young coconut shoots, both bold and punchy. Finish with green mango in syrup with tamarind sauce — the sweet-sour crunch is the house dessert that keeps people coming back.

Prices hover around 101–250 THB per person — reasonable for the quality of seafood and ingredients. Ordering a spread to share across the table gives best value. Open every day approximately 10:00–21:00, in a location slightly away from the main road but still easy to find and navigate. Parking is straightforward. The combination of consistent seasoning, fresh ingredients, and generous seating space keeps this restaurant popular.

Small note: opening hours can shift slightly day to day — check the restaurant page for updates. On long weekends the restaurant fills up, so calling ahead or arriving before the peak is advisable. Most dishes lean Southern Thai spicy; if you can't handle heat, tell the staff and they'll adjust. Wi-Fi is available and credit cards are accepted.
mustOrder: Green mango in syrup with tamarind sauce
blocks.bestFor: Family meals; groups; tasting bold Southern Ranong cooking

blocks.title: Know Before You Eat in Ranong

items.title: Getting Around
items.text: Ranong is small but the restaurants are spread out. Grab is scarce and unreliable here — renting a car or motorbike is the best move, or negotiate a price with a taxi or hire car in advance. Restaurants in the old quarter are walkable between each other; Pak Nam and Kapoe require driving.

items.title: Payment
items.text: Street food spots, som tam stalls, and the roti shop work mostly in cash — keep some small bills on you. Larger restaurants and some cafés accept PromptPay transfers, but credit cards are not widely accepted.

items.title: Beating the Queue
items.text: Dim sum and roti are morning foods — arrive before 09:00 to get the best selection before it sells out. Popular restaurants like Thod Rong Thao and Keinglay fill up fast on holiday evenings; come before or after the peak and you'll get a table much more easily.

items.title: The Heat
items.text: Southern Thai cooking in Ranong is genuinely fiery. If you can't handle serious spice, tell the restaurant and ask them to reduce the chillies. Ordering a steamed or lightly stir-fried seafood dish alongside the spicier plates helps balance the meal.

items.title: Language and Menus
items.text: Many local restaurants have Thai-only menus and limited English. Pointing at pictures or using a translation app works well. Key dish names to remember: bai liang pad khai (bai liang with egg), kung pad kapi sataw (prawns with shrimp paste and stink beans).

items.title: Tipping
items.text: No tipping is expected at local restaurants. Some sit-down spots include a service charge on the bill. A small tip for good service is always appreciated but never obligatory.

blocks.title: Plan Your Full Day of Eating in Ranong
blocks.html:
Start the morning with dim sum at Ranong O Cha — pick your own baskets from the chiller and add congee or steamed rice with preserved vegetables. If you're in the Ban Ngao area, swap that for Roti Nissara early in the morning, because the massaman roti and khao yam both sell out before noon. For lunch, try one of the Southern Thai restaurants: Khun Lin near Raksawarin Hot Spring has pla talumphuk and bai liang with egg; Thod Rong Thao in the old quarter is the go-to for prawns with shrimp paste and stink beans and soft-shell crab with garlic.

Save an afternoon window for a café. Baan Nai Mong Treehouse is ten minutes out of town — a creek-side treehouse café in the forest, the perfect place for a cold drink before the evening. Close the day with a sunset dinner by the sea at Keinglay in Pak Nam: order the yellow curry with sea bass and the steamed sea bass with lime while the sun drops over the Thai-Myanmar horizon. If you have more time, the drive to Kapoe for Baan Rai Ia Arun — khao nom jin with three dips beside a stream — is worth every kilometre. And if you need something bold and affordable for lunch, Pa Ratree Som Tam (Som Tam Dan) and her 3-flavour blue crab som tam is exactly that.

blocks.text: After a full day eating your way through Ranong, stay close to the best food — from hot-spring resorts to central town hotels near the markets and dim sum shops. Book in advance and you'll get a better price and the room you actually want.

faq.q: Which restaurant in Ranong is the most famous?
faq.a: By reputation and awards, Thod Rong Thao is one of the most talked-about Southern Thai restaurants in Ranong, winning consecutive Wongnai Users' Choice awards for its quality and honest cooking. Khun Lin is also a long-standing institution — over twenty years old — celebrated for its talum phuk fish and bai liang with egg. Both are perennial favourites.

faq.q: What are the signature local dishes to try in Ranong?
faq.a: Southern Thai staples like bai liang stir-fried with egg, prawns with shrimp paste and stink beans, and yellow curry with sea bass are on the menu at virtually every Southern Thai restaurant on this list. For fresh Andaman seafood, head to Keinglay in Pak Nam. Morning dim sum is at Ranong O Cha, and roti dipped in massaman curry is at Roti Nissara. These are the dishes that define eating in Ranong.

faq.q: How much does food in Ranong cost?
faq.a: Most dishes are reasonable. Som tam and roti stalls run around 40–100 THB per dish. An average Southern Thai restaurant meal comes to about 100–250 THB per person. Beachside seafood at somewhere like Keinglay runs higher — around 250–500 THB per person, especially if you're ordering whole fish.

faq.q: Do I need to book a table in advance?
faq.a: Most casual restaurants are walk-in. But on long weekends and on Saturday and Sunday evenings, popular spots like Thod Rong Thao and Keinglay fill up fast. If you're coming as a larger group or want a table by the sea at sunset, calling ahead is smart. For Roti Nissara, come early — it sells out rather than filling up.

faq.q: Which restaurants are open in the evening or late?
faq.a: Southern Thai and seafood restaurants are mostly open through the evening — Khun Lin closes around 20:00, Keinglay is ideal for an evening meal by the sea. Dim sum (Ranong O Cha) and roti (Roti Nissara) are breakfast spots — go in the morning. The café at Baan Nai Mong is open through the afternoon into early evening. Always check a restaurant's page before you head out, just to confirm.
